newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian stocks up but off highs as Chidambaram cheers.
newsitem.headline: Indian stocks up but off highs as Chidambaram cheers.

text.p: Indian stocks closed higher on Wednesday as former finance minister P. Chidambaram's return to the government spread cheer across markets, but profit-taking pared early gains, traders said.

"It's a good move and should boost investor confidence," said Aditya Rattan, chief representative at Daiwa Securities, referring to the decision by Chidambaram's Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) to rejoin the government.
TMC had earlier opted to stay out of the new government after its leader G.K. Moopanar was passed over as the choice for prime minister.
Government officials said Chidambaram was due to return to the cabinet as finance minister.
Bombay's benchmark index jumped nearly two percent to hit an early high of 3879.21 but eased to end 32.46 points, or 0.85 percent, higher at 3841.11.
"I think people took advantage of the early enthusiasm and decided to book profits in a strong market," said Maulik Sharedalal, broker at the Bombay Stock Exchange.
Traders said most funds stayed away from index-linked stocks preferring to hunt for bargains in secondliners.
Bombay's index has been range-bound during the past seven trading sessions as most investors opted to sit on the sidelines until Chidambaram returned.
"Investors like his aggression, his ability to take hard decisions," said a fund manager, citing Chidambaram's path-breaking federal budget announced on February 28.

Parliament on Wednesday opened a two-and-a-half week session to debate the 1997/98 (April-March) budget which slashed taxes, raised foreign portfolio limits in stocks of Indian companies and proposed that firms be allowed to buy back their shares.
"With the comeback of Chidambaram as finance minister, the financial budget would be passed without any major amendments," said Manoj Choraria of brokers Choraria Investments in Delhi.
In its cover story, "The Importance of Being Chidambaram," Outlook newsmagazine asked industrialists why so many people believed the former finance minister was indispensable to the economy.
"Chidambaram is a gentleman, he is easy to deal with, he is straightforward and progressive," responded Ratan Tata, who heads the giant Tata group.

Delhi's index closed 2.62 points higher at 801.24 -- off its early high of 815.40 -- as investors bought on hopes that Chidambaram would pilot the budget through parliament, despite opposition from left-wing parties and the right-wing opposition Bharatiya Janata Party.
On the National Stock Exchange (NSE), the index ended 22.60 points, or 2.14 percent, higher at 1080.05 in new-account trade.
Analysts said fundamental factors like falling interest rates, triggered by an easier central bank monetary policy announced this month, would also drive stocks higher.
"We expect interest rates to decline, especially at the long end, triggering a rally in stocks," Morgan Stanley analyst Pravin Shah said in a report.
Most banks have cut their prime lending rates to 14.0-16 percent from 14.5-17.5 percent.

Prateek Agarwal, deputy manager research at SBI Capital Markets, forecast Bombay's index would rise to 4,500 in the next three months as investors discounted poor company results for 1996/97 and looked ahead.
"There will be some sluggishness due to the results but then people will start looking at 1997/98 numbers and focus on interest rates which are close to all-time lows."
